questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How to research your own family history online
Research suggesting trees talk and help their families
Why forests are disappearing around the world so fast
The biggest and oldest trees in California's forests
questions.why: They discuss Suzanne Simard's view that trees are intelligent, communicate and recognise family members.

questions.q: What did Georgina do in her free time during lockdown?
options: She repainted her living room
She did exercise classes in the kitchen
She went for long walks in the woods
She researched her family history online
questions.why: She says she has been doing online research into her family history.

options: A network of underground roots linking related trees
A popular website about the world's famous forests
A type of spider that builds huge webs in woods
A map showing where the world's oldest trees grow
questions.why: Georgina describes it as the network of underground roots linking trees to others of the same family.

questions.q: According to Suzanne Simard, how do parent trees treat their own seedlings?
options: They block their sunlight so they grow slowly
They treat them exactly the same as strangers
They send them more nutrients than strangers
They leave them to grow alone without any help
questions.why: She agrees that parent trees send more nutrients to their offspring than to stranger trees.

questions.q: What happens when young trees receive extra nutrients and carbon?
options: They grow bigger root networks and grow faster
They produce more seeds straight away
They send the food back to the mother tree
They stop needing water
questions.why: They extend their root network, suck up more nutrients and increase their own growth.

questions.q: What does Suzanne Simard think many people wrongly believe about trees?
options: That they grow far too slowly to be worth studying
That they are much older than the human race
That they live together in family communities
That they are lifeless sticks that make no decisions
questions.why: She says people think of trees as sticks that don't change behaviours or make decisions.

questions.q: What do dying trees do, according to Neil?
options: They drop all of their seeds on the ground at once
They warn their offspring to make new root connections
They stop sharing food and water with other trees
They send poison through their roots to strangers
questions.why: Neil says before they die, they warn their offspring to start making new root connections.

questions.q: How does Georgina say the programme will change her walks in the woods?
options: She will stop walking there because it feels strange
She will collect seeds from the trees to plant at home
She will imagine the trees chatting to each other
She will measure the largest trees she walks past
questions.why: She says walks will feel different, surrounded by intelligent trees chatting to each other.
